Title: Polarization in (post)nomadic resource use in Eastern Morocco: insights using a multi-agent simulation model
Authors: Gunnar Dressler; Falk Hoffmann; Ingo Breuer; David Kreuer; Mohamed Mahdi; Karin Frank; Birgit Müller
Geographical_Context: High Plateau, Eastern Morocco
Agricultural_Domain: Pastoral livestock; Rangeland/common-property resource management; Social-ecological systems
Study_Objective: Use a spatially explicit multi-agent/agent-based model to identify economic, ecological, climatic and demographic drivers of socio-economic polarization among pastoralist households.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Simulate feedbacks among pastoralist households, livestock and common-property pastures to explain when polarization and poverty traps emerge under changing economic and environmental conditions.
Agent_Types: Pastoralist household agents
Agent_Roles: Choose grazing patches; manage herd size and monetary resources; pay living/mobility costs; destock animals when necessary; respond to pasture biomass and rainfall conditions.
Decision_Mechanism: Decision tree; Threshold-based livelihood and mobility rules; Rational pasture selection
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each household independently selects grazing patches and manages herd/mobility decisions using its own assets and full knowledge of pasture states; no central coordinator is modelled.
Input_Information: Herd size; Monetary resources; Pasture biomass; Distance/mobility cost; Living costs; Precipitation; Critical viable herd threshold
MAS_Platform_Technology: Structured ODD+D agent-based simulation; software platform NR
Coordination_Mechanism: Environment-mediated resource interaction; no explicit coordination protocol
Communication_Mechanism: Environment-mediated/indirect interaction through shared pasture states
Information_Shared: No direct messages; households perceive pasture biomass/state resulting from previous grazing decisions
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Common-property pasture biomass; Grazing access; Household mobility
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Secure household livelihood; Maintain herd above viable threshold; Access sufficient pasture biomass
Conflict_Resolution: NR
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Pastoralist households competing indirectly for limited grazing biomass and accessible pasture patches
Agricultural_Outcomes: Household herd-size dynamics; Livelihood viability; Socio-economic polarization; Monetary-resource trajectories
Livestock_Outcomes: Herd growth, destocking and collapse below critical viable herd-size thresholds
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: NR
Environmental_Outcomes: Pasture biomass dynamics and degradation; Effects of rainfall level/variability and grazing harshness on rangeland condition
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: NR
Quantitative_Results: NR
Tradeoffs_Reported: NR
Evaluation_Environment: Spatially explicit stylised common-property rangeland model approximating the High Plateau of Eastern Morocco; annual time steps over 200 years.
Data_Source: Empirical studies and household observations from Eastern Morocco; Previous simulation studies; Synthetic stochastic rainfall
Experimental_Scenarios: Household asset/mobility-cost heterogeneity; Ecological vegetation conditions; Climate and demographic change
Baselines_Comparators: Scenario/parameter comparisons; no single external baseline
Evaluation_Metrics: Degree of polarization; Herd-size classes; Monetary resources; Pasture biomass/system state
Evaluation_Results: NR
Evaluation_Scale: Multiple pastoralist households on a grid of 400-ha pasture patches; 200-year simulations; 500 runs per parameter combination
Limitation_Categories: Uncertainty; Real-world validation; Other — simplifying behavioural/economic assumptions
Reported_Limitations: Stylised virtual-lab model rather than quantitative prediction; households omit labour-force and preference differences, dynamic living costs and debt limits; mobility threshold and some behavioural responses are simplified.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Investigate household shocks and preferences; include labour and non-pastoral livelihood decisions; relax debt/living-cost and mobility assumptions; broaden behavioural realism.
Extraction_Notes: Households interact indirectly through shared pasture biomass rather than through explicit communication/negotiation; model is intended for mechanistic exploration, not quantitative forecasting.

Title: Smart Farming – Open Multi-agent Platform and Eco-System of Smart Services for Precision Farming

Title: Assessing seed and breeding interventions for organic farming using a multiagent value chain approach

Agricultural_Domain: Organic crop production; Seed systems and breeding; Agricultural value chains; Policy assessment

Decision_Mechanism: Mathematical optimisation; Dynamic linear programming; Heuristics; Adaptive expectations; Innovation-diffusion thresholds
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Heterogeneous agents make individual economic decisions using their own objective functions and constraints; no central decision controller determines all actor choices.
Input_Information: Farm characteristics; Seed prices and availability; Crop yields/prices; Production costs; Willingness to pay; Previous seed sales; Policy rules; Demand forecasts; Technical production constraints
MAS_Platform_Technology: GAMS 24.1; STATA15; VAL-MAS model; supplementary ODD/model documentation
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Materials and methods, pp.5–14; Fig.2; Additional-file model documentation referenced
Coordination_Mechanism: Value-chain supply-demand feedback; Market/price-mediated coordination; Recursive dynamic coupling across value-chain levels
Communication_Mechanism: Environment-mediated/indirect interaction through seed sales, prices, quantities and demand-supply feedback
Information_Shared: Seed demand/sales; Seed prices; Available quantities; Farm-gate prices; Production expectations; Policy conditions
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Organic seed supply and use; Seed-production capacity; Breeding/production budgets
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Farm and seed-multiplier gross-margin maximisation; Breeding revenue maximisation; Increase organic seed production/use under policy constraints
Conflict_Resolution: No explicit negotiation protocol; imbalances are resolved through market/supply constraints and each agent’s optimisation decisions.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Farm demand for organic seed versus limited seed-production capacity and technical constraints
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Model structure/interactions and adaptive expectations, pp.11–13; Fig.2
Agricultural_Outcomes: Organic seed adoption/use; Organic seed production; Farm-enterprise gross margins; Seed-multiplier gross margins; Breeding budgets
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Policy cost-effectiveness and improved matching of organic seed supply to demand
Environmental_Outcomes: NR
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: NR
Quantitative_Results: Under current conditions, phasing out derogations produced insufficient organic seed and about an 11% farm gross-margin loss. About €500/ha subsidy or €10/t carrot price premium was estimated to induce adoption across the full farm-agent population when supply is sufficient; improved germination could raise seed-multiplier gross margin by about 36%.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Policy/intervention cost vs organic-seed adoption; Seed availability/technical feasibility vs farm gross margin
Evaluation_Environment: VAL-MAS representation of the German organic wash/storage carrot seed value chain across breeding, seed multiplication and farming over eight model periods.
Data_Source: German farm accountancy data; National statistics; Stakeholder/expert interviews; Farmer survey; Market price/yield data; Technical databases; Expert assumptions
Experimental_Scenarios: Baseline plus phased derogation removal, improved germination/lygus control, sufficient-seed condition, organic-seed subsidy, farm-gate price premium and combined interventions; sensitivity analysis over alternative populations/prices/yields
Baselines_Comparators: Calibrated baseline reflecting current organic seed use; model validation against real-world statistics and expert judgement
Evaluation_Metrics: Organic seed use/production; Gross margins; Breeding budgets; Intervention cost; Diffusion/adopter group; Cost-effectiveness; Validation indicators
Evaluation_Results: Most baseline model outputs closely matched observed values; one Type-II seed-multiplier gross-margin validation showed a larger deviation; structural assumptions were additionally checked with experts.
Evaluation_Scale: 100 farm agents scaled to approximately 325 real producers; representative breeding and seed-multiplication actor types; 8 model periods; 10 generated farm-agent populations in sensitivity analysis
Limitation_Categories: Uncertainty; Reproducibility/data availability; Real-world validation; Other — case-study generalisability
Reported_Limitations: Single country-crop case and selected firms limit generalisability; some parameters rely on expert assumptions; organic-area expansion and conversion of non-organic farms are omitted; confidential/scarce economic data constrain parameterisation.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Adapt VAL-MAS to other crop-country cases; incorporate risk and external effects; improve evidence on seed-production stability and technical pest-control constraints; extend sustainability-related effects.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Verification/calibration/validation and scenarios, pp.13–17; Limitations/outlook, pp.23–24; Data availability, p.26
Extraction_Notes: Food industry and policy are exogenous rather than autonomous agents. Environmental benefits of organic farming are not modelled directly, so sustainability is coded Indirect.

Title: CowNet-AI: A Multi-Agent Decision Support Framework for Social Network–Driven Welfare Insights in Dairy Cattle
Authors: T. Shanteer; K. Sailunaz; S. R. Neethirajan
Geographical_Context: NR
Agricultural_Domain: Livestock/dairy; Animal welfare; Precision livestock farming
Study_Objective: Develop and pilot-test an explainable multi-agent conversational decision-support framework that combines dairy-cattle social network analysis, simulation, and research grounding to identify potential welfare risks.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Provide conversational, explainable decision support for identifying dairy-cattle social isolation and welfare-related risks using sensor-derived social-network information, simulation, and research evidence.
Agent_Types: Decision-support agents: Supervisor, Data Loader, SNA, Research, Simulation, Response, Report; Domain/simulation agents: Cow agents

Decision_Mechanism: LLM-based reasoning and intent routing; Conditional supervisor routing; Tool invocation; Rule/metric-based SNA reasoning
Agent_Autonomy_Description: The Supervisor autonomously determines query intent and selects specialist agents; specialist agents autonomously execute domain-specific tools and update shared GraphState, while final recommendations remain advisory and farmers retain decision authority.
Input_Information: Farmer natural-language queries; cow-location and interaction data; cow registry and pen assignments; SNA metrics; simulation outputs; research summaries; conversation history
MAS_Platform_Technology: LangGraph; LangChain; Python; FastAPI; NetworkX; LangSmith; OpenAI GPT-4o-mini
Interaction_Type: Communication; Information sharing; Cooperation; Coordination; Task allocation
Coordination_Mechanism: Centralised supervisor routing; Sequential specialist-agent orchestration; Shared-state coordination
Communication_Mechanism: Structured message passing; Shared GraphState; Indirect shared-state communication
Information_Shared: Conversation messages; cow-interaction data; SNA metrics; simulation outputs; research summaries; query context
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Farmer-query processing; Analytical and decision-support subtasks
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Correct/relevant query routing; efficient agent invocation; grounded and complete farmer response
Conflict_Resolution: Supervisor re-routes queries when prerequisites are missing and continues the workflow until sufficient information is available for a complete response.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: NA
Agricultural_Outcomes: NA
Livestock_Outcomes: Behaviour-based dairy-cattle welfare-risk and social-isolation indicators; identification of changes in social positioning and herd structure; farmer-facing early-warning recommendations; no clinically validated welfare outcome demonstrated.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: NA
Environmental_Outcomes: NA
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: NA
Quantitative_Results: NR
Tradeoffs_Reported: NR
Evaluation_Environment: Implemented CowNet-AI prototype evaluated using the MmCows dairy-cattle interaction dataset, synthetic behavioural simulation, and predefined natural-language farmer queries.
Data_Source: Public real-world sensor dataset; Synthetic simulation data; Generated evaluation queries
Experimental_Scenarios: MmCows week-to-week SNA analysis; isolation-risk queries; centrality queries; what-if simulations; general herd-management queries; report-generation queries; agent-ablation configurations
Baselines_Comparators: Single-agent GPT-4; Rule-based static SNA; CowNet-AI without Supervisor; CowNet-AI without Research Agent; CowNet-AI without Simulation Agent
Evaluation_Metrics: Task success; Intent-routing accuracy; Hallucination rate; Expert-rated relevancy; Query latency
Evaluation_Results: CowNet-AI achieved 100% intent-routing accuracy, 5/5 average expert-rated relevancy, 5% hallucination rate and approximately 58 s average query latency on the 20-query comparison. Full-system task success was 100%; removing the Research Agent reduced task success to 60%, removing the Simulation Agent to 85%, while single-agent GPT-4 and rule-based SNA achieved 50% and 35% task success respectively in the ablation comparison.
Evaluation_Scale: 7 specialised decision-support agents; MmCows dataset: 16 cows over 14 days; synthetic behavioural simulation: 20 cow agents; baseline comparison: 20 queries over 3 runs; agent-latency evaluation: 100 queries
Limitation_Categories: Scalability; Uncertainty; Explainability; Computational requirements; Real-world validation; Other — clinical validation/data representativeness; Other — LLM-evaluator bias
Reported_Limitations: Pilot-scale evaluation on a limited dataset; welfare risk is inferred from behavioural proxies without clinical ground truth; LLM-as-judge may introduce evaluation bias; residual hallucination remains; query latency and O(N²) SNA complexity limit scaling; shared GraphState may grow excessively; data quality and herd representativeness require further validation; no operational farm deployment.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Clinical/expert-in-the-loop welfare validation; multimodal integration of behaviour, vocalisation and health records; larger multi-site and longitudinal studies; scalability and real-time optimisation; privacy-preserving/federated approaches; improved uncertainty calibration and human verification; alternative edge/cloud deployment; sensor calibration and robust data-quality handling; integration with formal welfare-assessment frameworks.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Sections V–VII, pp.64889–64896; Figures 8–9; Table 4; Data and Code Availability
Extraction_Notes: Paper contains two distinct agent concepts: specialised LLM decision-support agents and autonomous cow agents used inside a behavioural simulator. The main MAS architecture is centrally orchestrated by the Supervisor via shared GraphState. Welfare outputs are behavioural early-warning indicators and are not clinically validated diagnoses.

Title: Peer-to-peer energy trading in dairy farms using multi-agent systems
Authors: Shah, Mian Ibad Ali; Wahid, Abdul; Barrett, Enda; Mason, Karl
Geographical_Context: Finland and Ireland dairy-farm communities
Agricultural_Domain: Dairy-farm energy management; Renewable energy; Peer-to-peer energy trading
Study_Objective: Develop and evaluate the MAPDES multi-agent P2P energy-trading simulator for dairy farms and quantify effects on electricity cost, sales revenue, peak grid demand and network size/configuration.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Enable dairy farms with renewable generation/storage to manage local energy and trade surplus/deficit electricity with peer farms through a distributed P2P market before using the utility grid.
Agent_Types: Farm/prosumer agents; Battery agents; Renewable-energy agents; Auctioneer/price-advisor agent; Energy-trader agents
Agent_Roles: Farms manage load, generation and battery use; buyers/sellers submit energy bids/offers; price advisor computes internal prices; auctioneer clears the market and settles unmatched quantities with the grid.
Decision_Mechanism: Rule-based load/battery management; Double auction; Supply-Demand-Ratio pricing; Market clearing
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each farm independently manages load, renewable generation and storage and controls its trading orders; a central auctioneer/advisor calculates prices and clears the market using limited shared information.
Input_Information: Farm load; PV/wind generation; Battery state of charge/capacity; Time-of-use and feed-in tariffs; Community supply-demand ratio; Bid/ask price and quantity
MAS_Platform_Technology: Python-based MAPDES simulator; System Advisor Model (SAM) for renewable-generation data
Coordination_Mechanism: Distributed P2P energy trading; Double-auction market; Central price advisor/auctioneer; Supply-demand pricing
Communication_Mechanism: Bid/ask and load/generation information exchanged through the auctioneer; distributed participant control with central market clearing
Information_Shared: Energy generation/load; Buy/sell quantities; Bid/ask prices; Internal buying/selling prices; Market-clearing outcomes
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Electricity/renewable energy; Battery storage; P2P energy trades
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Reduce electricity purchasing cost and peak grid demand; increase revenue/local renewable use; maximise market/social welfare while preserving participant privacy
Conflict_Resolution: Double-auction order matching clears compatible bids/offers; unmatched quantities are settled with the utility grid at tariff/feed-in prices.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Buyer and seller dairy farms/prosumers with time-varying energy surplus or deficit
Agricultural_Outcomes: Dairy-farm operational energy costs and grid-demand exposure improved; no milk-production outcome was evaluated.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Lower grid-energy purchases/peak demand; greater local renewable-energy utilisation; increased revenue from surplus energy sales
Environmental_Outcomes: NR
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Renewable-energy integration; P2P energy sharing; Battery storage; Peak-demand management
Quantitative_Results: Compared with the baseline without P2P/renewables, the reported strategy reduced electricity cost by 43%, reduced peak demand by 42%, and increased energy-sales revenue by 59%.
Tradeoffs_Reported: NR
Evaluation_Environment: MAPDES one-year hourly simulation of dairy-farm P2P energy communities using Finland and Ireland load/renewable-generation conditions.
Data_Source: Finnish measured/pre-recorded farm-load data; Irish farm-load model data; SAM PV-generation data; location-matched wind-generation data; battery specifications and electricity tariffs
Experimental_Scenarios: Different farm-community sizes; renewable-resource combinations; battery/PV/wind configurations; Finland vs Ireland; P2P vs non-P2P/renewable baselines; literature comparison; scalability/runtime analysis
Baselines_Comparators: No renewable energy/no P2P; Renewable energy without P2P; Related double-auction literature model
Evaluation_Metrics: Electricity purchasing cost; Electricity-sales revenue; Peak grid demand; Runtime/scalability
Evaluation_Results: MAPDES produced consistent beneficial trends across Finnish and Irish case datasets; execution time increased with community size while remaining suitable for the simulated hourly market process.
Evaluation_Scale: One-year simulations at 1-hour resolution; communities including 10, 20 and 50 farms depending on experiment; herd sizes approximately 20–150 cows; multiple RE configurations and two countries
Limitation_Categories: Scalability; Uncertainty; Real-world validation; Computational requirements; Other — incomplete information, line losses, privacy/security and behavioural assumptions
Reported_Limitations: Assumes rational market participants; real-time demand/price information may be incomplete; line losses are not fully represented; renewable variability, battery degradation, security/privacy and dynamic real-world market behaviour require further treatment.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Develop robust handling of incomplete information and line losses; investigate MARL/adaptive trading; model battery degradation; improve data security and real-world dynamic validation.
Extraction_Notes: S05 is the extended MAPDES journal study and is directly related to S29 (earlier MAPDES study) and S11 (later MARL extension); synthesis should avoid treating overlapping evidence as fully independent.

Evaluation_Environment: Usochicamocha district with 11 pump stations and 5,911 fields; combination of real field irrigation agents and district-scale virtual agents using real geospatial/weather/soil data.
