Authors: González-Briones, A.; Mezquita, Y.; Castellanos-Garzón, J.A.; Prieto, J.; Corchado, J.M.
Geographical_Context: Salamanca province, Spain
Agricultural_Domain: Irrigation/water management; Potato crop; Precision agriculture
Study_Objective: Design and evaluate a cloud-based multi-agent system that collects crop/sensor information and automatically adapts pivot irrigation to reduce water consumption in potato production.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Automate precision irrigation by fusing sensor/weather data, identifying zones with different water needs and controlling pivot irrigation actuators accordingly.
Agent_Types: Sensor Manager Agent; Actuator Manager Agent; Data Fusion Agent; Data Formatter Agent; Knowledge Extraction Agent; CBR Agent; Pivot agent
Agent_Roles: Sensor agents collect crop/environment data; persistence/fusion/formatter agents store and prepare information; AI agents cluster zones and derive decisions; actuator/pivot agents execute or simulate irrigation actions.
Decision_Mechanism: Clustering/unsupervised learning; Case-based reasoning; Penman-Monteith evapotranspiration and irrigation-requirement calculations; rule-based actuation
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Specialist agents automatically process sensing data and derive irrigation-zone decisions; the actuator manager opens the corresponding pivot electrovalves according to inferred crop needs.
Input_Information: Precipitation; soil moisture; air humidity; wind; solar radiation; crop coefficient; pesticides/fertilizers; historical logs; weather predictions
MAS_Platform_Technology: Cloud computing; WSN; RFID; Raspberry Pi 3 gateway; blockchain/cryptochip data transmission; CBR and clustering
Coordination_Mechanism: Centralised subsystem orchestration from sensing/data persistence through AI analysis to actuator control
Communication_Mechanism: Wireless sensor data transmission and inter-agent data flow through shared persistence/database subsystems
Information_Shared: Sensor measurements; historical logs; formatted/fused crop-zone data; inferred irrigation needs; actuator commands
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Irrigation water; Pivot irrigation scheduling/control
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Meet potato crop water requirements while reducing irrigation-water consumption and avoiding overwatering
Conflict_Resolution: Crop zones are classified by irrigation need and the actuator manager targets only zones requiring water, subject to pivot/time/efficiency constraints.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Crop zones with heterogeneous irrigation needs
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Evapotranspiration; precipitation/effective precipitation; soil moisture; humidity; wind; solar radiation; crop coefficient; irrigation efficiency; crop area and available irrigation time
Agricultural_Outcomes: Irrigation was adapted to potato crop water requirements; crop yield/quality was not experimentally measured.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: The proposed system reduced simulated pivot irrigation-water use relative to conventional pivot operation.
Environmental_Outcomes: Reduced freshwater use for irrigation; no broader environmental indicators evaluated.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Sensor-informed zone-specific irrigation and evapotranspiration-based water requirement estimation
Quantitative_Results: Simulated pivot water use decreased from 905.01 mm without the system to 768.63 mm with the MAS, a reported reduction of 15.06%.
Tradeoffs_Reported: NR
Evaluation_Environment: 20-ha sandy-loam potato-crop case study with a simulated linear pivot and real 2017 meteorological data
Data_Source: Real April–September 2017 meteorological data from Salamanca; crop/soil characteristics; simulated pivot and irrigation calculations
Experimental_Scenarios: Conventional pivot irrigation vs MAS-adjusted irrigation for a 150-day semi-late potato cycle
Baselines_Comparators: Traditional/conventional pivot irrigation without the proposed MAS
Evaluation_Metrics: Total irrigation depth/water use; evapotranspiration; irrigation frequency; required flow/pluviometry
Evaluation_Results: The MAS scenario reduced calculated irrigation-water consumption by 15.06% compared with conventional pivot irrigation.
Evaluation_Scale: 20 ha potato crop; 150-day crop cycle; simulated three-tower linear pivot; April–September 2017 weather conditions
Limitation_Categories: Real-world validation
Reported_Limitations: No substantive limitations discussion; evaluation is based on simulation using real meteorological data rather than an operational field deployment.
Reported_Research_Gaps: NR
Extraction_Notes: Despite wording that the architecture was tested in an agricultural environment, the described case study recreates pivot behaviour in simulation; therefore deployment is coded No.

Title: Challenges for Multi-Agent Based Agricultural Workforce Management
Authors: Harman, H.; Sklar, E.I.
Venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
Geographical_Context: Commercial soft-fruit farm; specific farm location NR
Agricultural_Domain: Harvest management; Agricultural workforce management; Soft-fruit production
Study_Objective: Evaluate multi-agent task-allocation and simulation methods for forming harvest teams and allocating picking tasks under incomplete/live farm data, while examining challenges to real-world deployment.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Assist farm managers in allocating human workers to fields and harvesting tasks to reduce staff time, balance workloads and improve use of a limited seasonal workforce.
Contribution_Type: Algorithm; Coordination mechanism; Simulation model; Decision-support method
Agent_Types: Fruit-picker/worker agents; Auction manager/task-allocation component
Agent_Roles: Worker agents represent individual pickers with fruit-specific picking speeds and execute simulated harvesting tasks; central allocation methods form teams and SSI auctions allocate/bundle in-field picking tasks.
Decision_Mechanism: Round-Robin team formation; iterative workload rebalancing; Sequential Single-Item auction; k-means worker modelling
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Picker agents independently compute bids/costs for picking tasks based on their schedules and capabilities, while central team-formation and auction mechanisms determine assignments.
Input_Information: Historic/live picking records; worker picking speeds; fruit type; worker availability; estimated/actual yield; field geometry; task locations; worker capacity
MAS_Platform_Technology: MASON multi-agent simulation; k-means clustering; statistical evaluation
Coordination_Mechanism: Round-Robin worker-to-field allocation with rebalancing; Sequential Single-Item auction for bundled harvesting tasks
Communication_Mechanism: Auction-based task announcement, bid computation and winner assignment within the simulator
Information_Shared: Task/field requirements; worker capabilities and picking speeds; bids/costs; assigned schedules; estimated yield and availability
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Seasonal human workforce; Harvesting/picking tasks; Worker-to-field assignments
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Minimise total staff time/payroll proxy; balance workload; complete harvesting efficiently with limited workers
Conflict_Resolution: Central team-allocation and auction mechanisms assign each worker/task according to estimated performance and bid cost; workload rebalancing moves workers between fields when it reduces imbalance.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Fields/tasks competing for limited workers; pickers competing for auctioned task bundles
Agricultural_Outcomes: Harvest workforce schedules/teams are generated for soft-fruit fields; direct crop-yield improvement is not measured.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Proposed teams can reduce total staff time, a proxy for labour/payroll cost; performance depends on data quality and worker-model assumptions.
Environmental_Outcomes: NR
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: NR
Quantitative_Results: Using historic data, proposed teams significantly reduced staff time but increased execution time versus actual teams. In live-data experiments, proposed teams improved both execution and staff time for two of three parameter settings; Table 1 reports 1,019–1,024 field/date samples per condition.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Staff-time/payroll reduction vs field execution time; allocation efficiency vs workload fairness; simulation realism vs worker privacy/data collection
Evaluation_Environment: MASON-based multi-agent simulation of commercial soft-fruit harvesting using actual field geometry, yields and worker performance records
Data_Source: Commercial-farm data from the 2021 picking season covering 182 picking days and 30 fields; historic records plus daily/live/prognostic yield and worker-availability data
Experimental_Scenarios: Historic vs live information; actual farm-manager teams vs proposed teams; three worker-clustering/default-speed parameter settings
Baselines_Comparators: Actual farm-manager-created teams; alternative clustering/default picking-speed settings
Evaluation_Metrics: Execution time; Staff time/payroll proxy; statistical significance using t-tests and ANOVA
Evaluation_Results: Historic-data proposed teams produced significantly shorter staff time but longer execution time. With live data, proposed teams improved both metrics for two parameter settings, but conclusions were affected by uncertain default speeds, yield estimates and worker availability.
Evaluation_Scale: 182 picking days; 30 fields; approximately 1,019–1,024 simulated field/date samples per experimental condition
Limitation_Categories: Uncertainty; Real-world validation; Reproducibility/data availability; Adoption/usability
Reported_Limitations: Simulation omits some real worker behaviours such as walking/break detail; default picking speeds for unseen worker-fruit combinations are uncertain; estimated yield and worker-availability lists can be inaccurate; intrusive tracking raises worker/privacy acceptance concerns.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Deploy proposed team allocations on a commercial farm; improve the simulator with deployment data; test additional task-allocation mechanisms/parameters; evaluate hybrid human-robot workforces.
Extraction_Notes: Related to S33 and S34 in the Harman–Sklar harvest-workforce/task-allocation research line; overlapping datasets/methods should not be counted as independent evidence during synthesis.

PDF_Filename: Assessing Adaptive Irrigation Impacts on Water Scarcity in Nonstationary Environments—A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach.pdf
Title: Assessing Adaptive Irrigation Impacts on Water Scarcity in Nonstationary Environments—A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
Authors: Hung, F.; Yang, Y.C.E.
Geographical_Context: Colorado River Basin, Western United States and Mexico
Agricultural_Domain: Irrigation/water management; Agricultural water demand; Coupled human-water system
Study_Objective: Develop an RL-based agent model of adaptive agricultural water demand and assess how changing irrigation behaviour affects regional water scarcity under nonstationary conditions.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Simulate adaptive agricultural water-demand decisions and assess their effects on Colorado River Basin water scarcity under changing hydroclimatic conditions.
Agent_Types: Agricultural water-user agents; Farms; Irrigation ditches; Irrigation districts; Tribal water users; Groups of farming entities
Agent_Roles: Observe water-system information; determine requested changes in annual water diversion; submit diversion requests; learn from received water and shortage feedback; update future water-demand policies.
Decision_Mechanism: Reinforcement learning; Farmer's Q-Learning (Q-learning variant); ε-greedy action selection; POMDP
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each agricultural water-user agent independently adjusts its requested annual diversion based on its learned Q-function, perceived water availability and previous feedback; actual water delivery remains constrained by CRSS allocation rules and physical availability.
Input_Information: Current/received water diversion; perceived water availability; historical diversion experience; winter precipitation for Upper Basin agents; Lake Mead water level for Lower Basin agents; learned transition probabilities and previous rewards
MAS_Platform_Technology: Python 3.6; Colorado River Simulation System (CRSS)
Coordination_Mechanism: Environment-mediated coordination; CRSS water-allocation rules
Communication_Mechanism: Indirect/environment-mediated agent–CRSS feedback; no direct agent-agent communication reported
Information_Shared: Agent diversion requests to CRSS; actual water received; future water-availability information returned through the model environment.
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Irrigation water / river-basin water allocation
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Agent utility maximisation through adaptive water-diversion decisions; basin allocation according to CRSS rules
Conflict_Resolution: CRSS water-allocation rules and physical water availability determine the water delivered when requested diversion exceeds available supply; shortages feed back into subsequent agent learning.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: 78 agricultural water-user agents drawing from the shared Colorado River Basin water system.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Current diversion; water received; expected/future water availability; winter precipitation; Lake Mead elevation; learned experience/Q-values; shortage feedback
Agricultural_Outcomes: Adaptive irrigation-water diversion/demand behaviour under changing water availability; no direct crop-yield or farm-productivity outcome evaluated.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Agricultural water users can learn to reduce subsequent diversion under persistent shortage conditions; Lower Basin agents show reduced water use after learning from drought/shortage feedback.
Environmental_Outcomes: Regional water scarcity; reservoir water levels/storage; basin water consumption/depletion; reliability of water delivery to Mexico
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Adaptive reduction of agricultural water demand through learning; soft-policy scenarios influencing water-user behaviour through education/stakeholder engagement
Quantitative_Results: ABM-CRSS predicts Lakes Powell and Mead becoming depleted around 2034 under the examined drier-than-normal future scenario. Water delivery shortage to Mexico can occur as early as 2033 in ABM-CRSS, compared with approximately 2044 in the original CRSS. Lower Basin agents subsequently reduce water use after learning from persistent shortage conditions.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Agricultural water demand vs basin water security/reservoir storage
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Sections 4.3–4.4, pp.14–16; Section 5.1, pp.17–18; Section 6, pp.18–19
Evaluation_Environment: Two-way coupled RL-ABM and Colorado River Simulation System representing the Colorado River Basin.
Data_Source: Historical water diversion/depletion data; Lake Mead water-level data; PRISM precipitation data; CRSS hydrological data; Monte Carlo-generated training states; Simulation-generated future conditions
Experimental_Scenarios: Historical training/testing; drier-than-normal 2019–2060 scenario; RL-ABM coupled to CRSS; ABM with learning disabled; original CRSS; 100 stochastic future simulations; soft-policy scenarios S1 and S2
Baselines_Comparators: Original CRSS; ABM-No RL
Evaluation_Metrics: Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE); Pearson correlation; mean and standard-deviation ratios; MAE; RMSE; annual diversion/depletion; reservoir level/storage; Mexico water delivery; shortage occurrence
Evaluation_Results: Historical water-diversion behaviour was validated against observations using KGE/correlation/error metrics; learning and no-learning/baseline configurations produced distinct future water-demand and shortage trajectories.
Evaluation_Scale: 78 agricultural water-user agents: 56 Upper Basin and 22 Lower Basin; 49 water-user groups; historical calibration/testing using 1971–2018 data; 2019–2060 future simulation; 100 repeated stochastic coupled-model simulations
Limitation_Categories: Uncertainty; Reproducibility/data availability; Real-world validation; Other — simplified human decision model
Reported_Limitations: Upper Basin observations are available mainly at sub-basin rather than individual-agent level; some Lower Basin agents have short records; agent parameter uncertainty affects classification and results; climate-input and model-structure uncertainty are incompletely represented; agent decisions are simplified to diversion and water information; production costs, crop demand, water-saving technology and broader socioeconomic factors are omitted; group-level agents may not reproduce individual preferences; political responses are not represented.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Improve agent-level diversion and shortage-allocation data; incorporate climate and model-structure uncertainty; include physical and socioeconomic decision factors; use survey/first-hand behavioural data; introduce additional water-user types such as municipal and industrial agents; incorporate crop economic values and production functions; evaluate newer CRSS policies including the 2019 Drought Contingency Plan.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Sections 3.3–3.4, pp.8–10; Section 4, pp.10–16; Sections 5–6, pp.17–19; Data Availability Statement, p.19
Extraction_Notes: Agents represent aggregated agricultural water users rather than necessarily individual farmers. Coordination is primarily environment/CRSS-mediated rather than direct agent-agent communication. Real historical data are used, but the MAS itself is simulation-based.

PDF_Filename: Multi-agent agro-economic simulation of irrigation water demand with climate services for climate change adaptation.pdf
Title: Multi-agent agro-economic simulation of irrigation water demand with climate services for climate change adaptation
Authors: Balbi, S.; Bhandari, S.; Gain, A.K.; Giupponi, C.
Geographical_Context: Venice Lagoon Watershed, north-east Italy
Agricultural_Domain: Irrigation/water management; Climate-change adaptation; Farm economics/crop allocation
Study_Objective: Develop a prototype multi-agent agro-economic model to explore how heterogeneous farmer decisions, irrigation systems and climate-service quality affect future irrigation-water demand and farm income under climate change.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Simulate autonomous farmer adaptation to seasonal/bi-weekly climate information and quantify consequences for crop allocation, irrigation water demand and farm income from 2015–2030.
Agent_Types: Farmer agents
Agent_Roles: Farmers choose crop allocation and irrigation management based on risk attitude, climate forecasts, crop economics and irrigation-system characteristics; farm economic state evolves over time.
Decision_Mechanism: Fuzzy risk-attitude classification; forecast-informed crop-allocation rules; FAO-56 soil-water-balance irrigation rules; stochastic economic decisions
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each farmer independently adapts crop allocation and irrigation decisions to forecasts, risk attitude, farm income and irrigation technology; direct farmer-to-farmer learning is not implemented in the prototype.
Input_Information: Seasonal and bi-weekly climate forecasts; precipitation/evapotranspiration; crop prices and production costs; farmer age/income/risk attitude; irrigation-system efficiency/cost; soil-water state
MAS_Platform_Technology: Simile; UML/ODD+D conceptual modelling; FAO-56 soil-water balance; COSMO-CLM climate projections
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Materials and methods; model structure/process sections, pp.176–181
Coordination_Mechanism: No explicit inter-farmer coordination in the implemented prototype; farmers respond independently to shared climate-service information and environmental conditions
Communication_Mechanism: Climate-service-to-farmer information broadcast; direct farmer-to-farmer communication/learning not implemented
Information_Shared: Seasonal rainfall forecast; bi-weekly weather information; climate uncertainty
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Irrigation water; Crop/land allocation
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Adapt crop and irrigation decisions to protect farmer income while responding to water availability/climate risk
Conflict_Resolution: NA
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Multiple farmers collectively contribute to territorial irrigation-water demand, but explicit competition/allocation among them is not implemented.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Forecast precipitation; crop water balance; crop type; irrigation-system efficiency and cost; farmer risk attitude; climate-service uncertainty
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Materials and methods; tactical/strategic decision sections, pp.176–181
Agricultural_Outcomes: Climate forecasts and farmer risk attitudes alter maize/wheat land allocation; farm income changes with forecast quality and irrigation technology.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Irrigation-water withdrawals vary by irrigation-system efficiency and climate-service accuracy; lower-efficiency systems show greater withdrawal variability.
Environmental_Outcomes: Future irrigation-water demand/water-scarcity pressure under climate change is explicitly modelled.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Forecast-informed crop and irrigation adaptation; comparison of drip, sprinkler and gravity irrigation systems; climate services supporting adaptive management
Quantitative_Results: Nine scenario sets of 100 simulations were run with cohorts of 25 farmers. Forecast uncertainty levels of ±10%, ±30% and ±90% were explored; exact effect sizes for water withdrawal/income are not reported numerically in the text.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Water withdrawals and irrigation-system efficiency vs farm income; adaptation benefits vs risk from inaccurate climate forecasts
Evaluation_Environment: Prototype Simile model of 25 heterogeneous farmer agents in the Venice Lagoon Watershed using a 2015–2030 climate scenario
Data_Source: COSMO-CLM/IPCC A1B climate projection; Venice Lagoon Watershed data; INEA farm/economic references; crop/irrigation parameters; some exploratory parameters based on authors’ experience/reference values
Experimental_Scenarios: Three irrigation systems (drip, sprinkler, gravity) crossed with three climate-forecast uncertainty levels; 2015–2030 simulation under one A1B climate scenario
Baselines_Comparators: Scenario comparison across irrigation technologies and climate-service uncertainty levels; no conventional non-agent baseline
Evaluation_Metrics: Overall irrigation-water withdrawals; Farmer income; Crop/land allocation; distribution/variability of outcomes
Evaluation_Results: Poorer climate forecasts increased variability of water withdrawals and reduced farmer incomes; inefficient irrigation systems showed greater instability. Results demonstrate joint exploration of autonomous farmer adaptation and planned climate-service adaptation.
Evaluation_Scale: 25 farmer agents; 16-year period (2015–2030); nine scenario sets × 100 simulation runs
Limitation_Categories: Uncertainty; Scalability; Real-world validation; Environmental modelling; Reproducibility/data availability
Reported_Limitations: Prototype/toy model; farmer-to-farmer learning and effects of bad decisions not implemented; no explicit spatial variability; only one climate scenario; parameters and modules require further calibration/validation; Simile may not scale to the full intended multi-agent spatial model.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Add individual/collective learning and farmer interaction; include heterogeneous soils and multiple climate scenarios; integrate GIS/spatially explicit modelling; strengthen sensitivity, calibration, validation and uncertainty/error-propagation analysis; consider migration to an agent-based platform.
Extraction_Notes: Implemented prototype behaves more like a multi-agent micro-simulation than a fully interacting MAS because direct farmer-to-farmer learning/coordination is designed conceptually but not yet implemented.

PDF_Filename: A multi-agent simulation model for spatial optimisation of manure allocation.pdf
Title: A multi-agent simulation model for spatial optimisation of manure allocation
Authors: van der Straeten, B.; Buysse, J.; Nolte, S.; Lauwers, L.; Claeys, D.; van Huylenbroeck, G.
Venue: Journal of Environmental Planning and Management
Geographical_Context: Flanders, Belgium
Agricultural_Domain: Livestock manure management; Nutrient management; Environmental planning; Manure transport and processing
Study_Objective: Develop a spatial mathematical-programming multi-agent simulation of manure production, disposal, transport and processing across the Flemish farm population to evaluate policy and support cost-efficient processing investment decisions.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Optimise spatial manure allocation among own-land application, transport to other farms and processing while respecting nutrient regulations and minimising allocation costs.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; Optimisation method; Decision-support system; Policy-analysis framework
Agent_Types: Farmer agents; Municipal manure-transport firm entities
Agent_Roles: Farmer agents choose manure disposal, transport and processing quantities under legal/economic constraints; municipal transport firms aggregate local supply/demand and optimise inter-municipal manure exchange.
Decision_Mechanism: Mathematical programming; Cost minimisation; Constrained manure-balance optimisation; Shadow-price/dual-value analysis
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each farm independently optimises manure-management choices subject to farm-specific nutrient, land and policy constraints; inter-municipal exchanges are coordinated at a higher transport-firm level.
Input_Information: Farm manure production; nutrient/emission rights; crop/land area; fertiliser use; manure type; transport distance/cost; processing cost/capacity; legal processing obligations
MAS_Platform_Technology: GAMS; Mathematical Programming-based Multi-Agent Simulation (MP-MAS)
Interaction_Type: Information sharing; Coordination; Competition; Resource allocation
Coordination_Mechanism: Hierarchical farm-to-municipality manure market optimisation; constrained transport/processing allocation
Communication_Mechanism: Indirect market/optimisation-mediated interaction through hypothetical municipal transport firms; explicit messaging protocol NR
Information_Shared: Farm manure surplus/demand; transport flows; processing demand/capacity; nutrient rights; allocation costs; regional marginal disposal costs
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Manure/nutrients; Agricultural land disposal capacity; Manure-processing capacity; Manure transport
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Minimise manure transport/processing/allocation costs while satisfying nutrient-application limits and processing obligations; identify cost-efficient processing locations.
Conflict_Resolution: Constrained mathematical optimisation balances manure supply and demand across farms/municipalities and routes surplus to transport or processing when own-land disposal limits are reached.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Livestock farms competing for geographically limited manure-disposal/emission-right capacity and processing capacity.
Agricultural_Outcomes: Farm-level manure-management choices and processing-investment needs are estimated; no crop-yield or animal-performance outcome is evaluated.
Livestock_Outcomes: No direct animal-production or welfare outcome is evaluated; livestock manure production is represented as the pollution/source term.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Optimised manure transport and processing locations/capacities; lower total allocation cost under market-driven processing; improved transparency of regional processing demand.
Environmental_Outcomes: Nitrogen/manure surplus, over-fertilisation pressure and location-specific marginal pollution-abatement pressure are represented; direct water-quality concentrations are not simulated.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Legal nutrient-application limits; manure transport to deficit areas; manure processing; spatial targeting of additional processing capacity; regional manure-pressure indicator.
Quantitative_Results: For 2006 the model estimated 26.40 million kg N processing demand versus about 16.3–16.4 million kg N existing processing, leaving about 10.1 million kg N additional demand. Market-driven processing reduced total allocation cost by €2,399,330 relative to obligatory processing; net transport-flow and processing-behaviour validation correlations were r=0.809 and r=0.786 (p<0.001).
Tradeoffs_Reported: Environmental/regulatory compliance vs farmer allocation cost; manure transport vs processing; mandatory policy steering vs market-driven cost efficiency.
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Model validation; Policy analysis
Evaluation_Environment: Flemish manure market represented at individual-farm and municipal levels with farm manure production, land disposal, transport and processing decisions.
Data_Source: Flemish Land Agency administrative database: manure production, transactions, nutrient acquisition/use and farm characteristics for 2000–2006; 2006 farm population used for the main case.
Experimental_Scenarios: Mandatory-processing policy vs market-driven processing; optimisation of additional processing capacity/location; regional manure-pressure indicator analysis; current-capacity scenario.
Baselines_Comparators: Observed manure transport/processing behaviour for validation; obligatory-processing policy vs market-driven processing; current operational processing capacity.
Evaluation_Metrics: Pearson correlation with observed flows/processing; total manure-allocation cost; processed nitrogen; processing-capacity gap; transport/processing demand; regional manure-pressure shadow price.
Evaluation_Results: The model reproduced observed net transport and processing behaviour with high correlations, identified a substantial processing-capacity gap, and showed that market-driven allocation could meet nutrient limits at lower cost than obligatory processing.
Evaluation_Scale: 38,777 farms from a 60,577-farm administrative database; 308 municipalities; four manure types; main simulation year 2006.
Limitation_Categories: Environmental modelling; Computational requirements; Real-world validation; Other — normative/static farm-decision assumptions
Reported_Limitations: Model focuses only on manure management and ignores interactions with other farm decisions such as crop choice; it is normative/comparative-static rather than behavioural-dynamic; within-year timing/environmental effects are outside scope; large-scale farm interaction creates substantial computational demands.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Develop a positive/behavioural version for farmer responses to policy change; integrate manure management with broader whole-farm decisions; extend temporal/environmental dynamics and apply the MP-MAS approach to other spatial pollution/resource problems.
Extraction_Notes: Large-scale MP-MAS uses hypothetical municipal transport firms as computational aggregation entities while retaining individual farm optimisation; environmental outcomes concern manure/nitrogen pressure rather than directly simulated water-quality concentrations.

PDF_Filename: A Multi-Agent Systems Approach for Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading in Dairy Farming.pdf
Title: A Multi-agent Systems Approach for Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading in Dairy Farming
Authors: Shah, M.I.A.; Wahid, A.; Barrett, E.; Mason, K.
Venue: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Geographical_Context: NR (simulation-based dairy-farm community; no operational farm location specified)
Agricultural_Domain: Dairy-farm energy management; Renewable energy; Peer-to-peer energy trading
Study_Objective: Develop MAPDES, a MAS-based distributed P2P energy-trading simulator for dairy farms using renewable generation, batteries, an internal price advisor and auction-based market clearing.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Coordinate dairy-farm prosumers to trade surplus renewable electricity locally, manage batteries and reduce grid dependence, energy cost and peak demand.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; Platform/framework; Coordination mechanism; Decision-support method
Agent_Types: Dairy-farm/prosumer agents; Battery agents/components; Trader agents; Central auctioneer/price-advisor component
Agent_Roles: Farm prosumers manage load, renewable generation and batteries and decide whether to buy/sell; the price advisor calculates internal prices; the auctioneer clears P2P trades.
Decision_Mechanism: Rule-based load/battery management; Supply-Demand-Ratio pricing; Auction-based market clearing
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each farm independently manages generation, demand and battery state and submits buy/sell needs, while a central auctioneer/advisor calculates market prices and clears trades.
Input_Information: Farm load; PV/wind generation; battery state of charge and charge/discharge limits; time-of-use grid tariff; feed-in tariff; community supply-demand ratio; energy surplus/deficit
MAS_Platform_Technology: Python; System Advisor Model (SAM) generation data; MAPDES simulator
Coordination_Mechanism: Distributed P2P trading with central price advisor/auctioneer; Supply-Demand-Ratio pricing; auction-based market clearing
Communication_Mechanism: Farm agents share generation/load and buy/sell information with the central auctioneer/advisor for market clearance.
Information_Shared: Energy generation/load; surplus/deficit; buy/sell quantities; internal buying/selling prices; market-clearing outcomes
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Electricity/renewable energy; Battery storage; P2P energy trades; Peak grid demand
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Reduce electricity purchase cost, peak grid demand and grid dependence; increase local renewable use and revenue from surplus energy sales.
Conflict_Resolution: Auction-based market clearing matches local surplus and deficit; unmatched energy is bought from or sold to the utility grid.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Dairy-farm prosumers with time-varying electricity surplus/deficit compete/cooperate in the local energy market.
Agricultural_Outcomes: Dairy-farm operating energy cost and grid-demand exposure are reduced; no milk-production or animal-performance outcome is evaluated.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Lower grid-energy purchases and peak demand; greater local renewable-energy utilisation; increased revenue from surplus-energy sales.
Environmental_Outcomes: Greater use/trading of renewable electricity and reduced grid dependence; carbon-emission reduction is motivated but not directly quantified.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: On-farm renewable generation; battery storage; P2P energy sharing; peak-demand management.
Quantitative_Results: RE+P2P farms paid about 30% less than the no-RE/no-P2P baseline. With RE present, P2P reduced community energy-purchasing cost by about 1%, reduced peak-hour grid demand by 24%, and increased earnings from energy sales by about 37% relative to no P2P.
Tradeoffs_Reported: NR
Evaluation_Environment: One-year hourly simulation of a dairy-farm prosumer community with loads, PV/wind generation, batteries, utility-grid settlement and P2P market clearing.
Data_Source: Farm-load dataset from Uski et al.; PV and wind generation data from System Advisor Model (SAM); simulated battery and market states.
Experimental_Scenarios: 10 prosumer farms simulated for one year at one-hour resolution; RE+P2P compared with no-RE/no-P2P and RE/no-P2P configurations.
Baselines_Comparators: No renewable energy and no P2P trading; Renewable energy without P2P trading.
Evaluation_Metrics: Energy purchased/cost; peak-hour grid demand; energy sold/revenue; internal selling/buying prices.
Evaluation_Results: The simulated P2P market consistently reduced grid dependence and peak demand and increased local surplus-energy value; no separate algorithmic accuracy/robustness benchmark was reported.
Evaluation_Scale: 10 prosumer dairy farms; one year; one-hour time step.
Limitation_Categories: Real-world validation; Environmental modelling; Other — simplified market/network assumptions
Reported_Limitations: Evaluation is simulation-only; line losses are not represented and load/battery management does not yet adapt to bidding prices; the model therefore simplifies real market/network behaviour.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Investigate the influence of bidding prices on load/battery management; incorporate line losses; use MARL to improve market estimation and decision-making.
Extraction_Notes: Earlier MAPDES publication in the SF05 family; S05 provides a more extensive MAS/P2P evaluation and S11 later extends the line with MARL.

PDF_Filename: Heterogeneous multi-agent resource allocation through multi-bidding with applications to precision agriculture.pdf
Title: Heterogeneous multi-agent resource allocation through multi-bidding with applications to precision agriculture
Authors: Cobbenhagen, A.T.J.R.; Antunes, D.J.; van de Molengraft, M.J.G.; Heemels, W.P.M.H.
Geographical_Context: Wageningen, Netherlands — historical 1991 weather data used in simulation
Agricultural_Domain: Crop production; Irrigation/water management; Precision agriculture
Study_Objective: Develop a scalable multi-bidding optimisation framework for allocating resources and heterogeneous agricultural agents while maximising farm profit.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Schedule the time, location, and quantity of resources delivered by heterogeneous agricultural agents to crop subfields while maximising whole-farm profit.
Agent_Types: Agricultural resource-delivery agents; Irrigation agents
Agent_Roles: Deliver resources to crop subfields; select feasible client bids; allocate resource-delivery tasks subject to agent capacity constraints.
Decision_Mechanism: Approximate dynamic programming; Multi-bidding; Mixed-integer bilinear optimisation
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Clients independently compute multiple candidate resource bids; the agent group selects bids and allocates delivery tasks subject to resource and capacity constraints.
Input_Information: Client/crop state; expected product gain; resource requirements and costs; agent capacities; product prices; disturbance/weather information
MAS_Platform_Technology: MATLAB; SCIP; LINTUL2 crop-growth model
Interaction_Type: Communication; Information sharing; Coordination; Task allocation
Coordination_Mechanism: Multi-bidding; Constrained optimisation
Communication_Mechanism: Client-to-agent bid transmission; communication protocol NR
Information_Shared: Expected future product gain; expected future resource use; requested current resource quantity
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Water; Fertiliser; Pesticides; Agricultural-agent scheduling
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Profit maximisation
Conflict_Resolution: The constrained MIBP selects one feasible bid per client and assigns agents/resources while enforcing capacity and allocation constraints.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Crop subfields competing for limited agricultural-agent service capacity; simulation: 30 subfields sharing 3 irrigation agents.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Crop state; soil-water state; crop growth response; rainfall; temperature; irradiation; resource demand/bids; irrigation-agent capacity
Agricultural_Outcomes: Spring-wheat yield = 6.739 t/ha DM with the proposed approach; 88% of theoretical maximum yield.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Proposed allocation used 1,358 reported units of irrigation water while producing 6.739 t/ha DM; theoretical maximum yield would require 11,909 units of water.
Environmental_Outcomes: NR
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: NR
Quantitative_Results: Proposed: 1,358 resource units; 6.739 t/ha DM yield; €2.02×10^6 profit. No irrigation: 0 resource units; 5.215 t/ha; €1.56×10^6. Proposed profit increased by 29% relative to no irrigation and achieved 88% of theoretical maximum yield.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Crop yield vs irrigation requirement/profit
Evaluation_Environment: Simulated spring-wheat farm using the LINTUL2 crop-growth model and constrained irrigation-agent allocation.
Data_Source: Historical weather data; Simulation-generated crop/resource data
Experimental_Scenarios: Theoretical maximum-yield irrigation; No irrigation; Proposed multi-bidding allocation
Baselines_Comparators: No irrigation; Theoretical field-capacity / maximum-yield scenario
Evaluation_Metrics: Irrigation resource use; Crop yield; Farm profit
Evaluation_Results: NR
Evaluation_Scale: 30 equal-sized subfields; 3 irrigation agents; 1 crop/product; 1 resource (water); agents allocatable twice per day; one growing season
Limitation_Categories: Environmental modelling; Real-world validation; Other — bid/model assumptions
Reported_Limitations: Performance depends strongly on bid quality; crop dynamics are simplified; simulation assumes arbitrary agent capacities/cost parameters; temporal resource ordering and whole-season resource constraints are not fully represented; evaluation is simulation-based.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Improve bid quality through client communication; investigate alternative bidding/base policies; study relation to knapsack optimisation; use more comprehensive crop-growth models; model temporal resource-ordering constraints; include resource constraints over the complete growing season; investigate realistic cost parameters.
Extraction_Notes: Multi-bidding is not treated as negotiation/auction: bids are alternative client resource scenarios selected by a constrained optimiser. Precision agriculture is an application of a general D-H-MARA framework, and evaluation is simulation-only.

PDF_Filename: Dynamic Task Allocation Method for Heterogenous Multiagent System in Uncertain Scenarios of Agricultural Field Operation.pdf
Title: Dynamic Task Allocation Method for Heterogenous Multiagent System in Uncertain Scenarios of Agricultural Field Operation
Authors: Liang, Y.; Zhou, K.; Wu, C.
Geographical_Context: Generic agricultural field-operation scenarios; no specific geographical case study
Agricultural_Domain: Agricultural robotics/machinery; Field operations; Dynamic task allocation
Study_Objective: Develop a robust and efficient dynamic task-allocation method for heterogeneous agricultural multi-agent teams under agent, task and capability uncertainty.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Dynamically allocate agricultural field strips/tasks to heterogeneous autonomous agents so that field work remains efficient when agents/tasks enter, leave, fail or change capability.
Agent_Types: Heterogeneous autonomous agricultural field-operation agents/robots; Temporary auctioneer-role agents
Agent_Roles: Agents execute field strips and can enter/leave or change capability; the highest-capability candidate becomes auctioneer and allocates favourable task blocks through adaptive auctions.
Decision_Mechanism: Heuristic-Based Clustering Auction (HBCA); capability-priority auctioneer selection; heuristic task clustering; Potential Field of Capability Influence; adaptive auction
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Agents execute assigned strips autonomously; candidate agents are dynamically reordered by capability, and allocation is recomputed when agents/tasks or capabilities change.
Input_Information: Agent capabilities; agent availability; field-strip completion/assignment states; task additions/removals; capability changes; field-block sizes; travel/nonoperating cost parameters
MAS_Platform_Technology: C# simulation
Coordination_Mechanism: Heuristic-Based Clustering Auction; capability-priority auctioneer selection; adaptive reallocation under six uncertainty scenarios
Communication_Mechanism: Auction/state exchange among agents and task blocks; implementation-level communication protocol NR
Information_Shared: Agent capability/availability; strip/task state; field-block bids; assignment state; uncertainty events
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Agricultural field strips/tasks for planting, spraying or harvesting; heterogeneous robot/vehicle capability and operating time
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Maximise total allocation reward and minimise nonoperating/travel time while completing all tasks under dynamic uncertainty.
Conflict_Resolution: Adaptive auctions and PFCI-based reclustering/reallocation move overloaded or newly available task blocks to suitable agents after failures, additions or capability changes.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Heterogeneous agricultural agents compete for/are matched to field blocks according to capability while multiple strips require completion.
Agricultural_Outcomes: Field-operation tasks are completed under changing agent/task conditions; no crop-yield outcome is evaluated.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Substantially lower nonoperating/travel time and more robust dynamic reallocation than comparator MRTA algorithms.
Environmental_Outcomes: NR
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: NR
Quantitative_Results: Across 36 uncertainty instances, HBCA reduced average nonoperating time by 69.36% versus MIG, 68.94% versus RSSIA and 47.79% versus LQM auction.
Tradeoffs_Reported: NR
Evaluation_Environment: Synthetic agricultural-field strip allocation with heterogeneous autonomous agents under dynamic uncertainty.
Data_Source: Simulation-generated agents/tasks and uncertainty events.
Experimental_Scenarios: Six uncertainty types: agent removal/addition, task removal/addition, and agent-capability decrease/increase; q=50 or 100 tasks and m=5, 10 or 15 agents.
Baselines_Comparators: MIG; RSSIA; LQM auction
Evaluation_Metrics: Average nonoperating time; Relative Percentage Reduction (RPR)
Evaluation_Results: HBCA achieved the lowest average nonoperating time in all 36 tested instances and outperformed all three comparator algorithms, especially when agent capabilities differed substantially.
Evaluation_Scale: 16 candidate agents; six subsets with 50/100 tasks and 5/10/15 active agents; 36 uncertain instances.
Limitation_Categories: Real-world validation; Other — simplified synthetic task/motion assumptions
Reported_Limitations: NR
Reported_Research_Gaps: NR
Extraction_Notes: Auction is decentralised through dynamically selected agent auctioneers; field blocks act as bidders/task entities rather than autonomous agricultural agents. Reported setup assumes equal task priorities, identical turning behaviour and synthetic uncertainty.

PDF_Filename: A constrained multi-agent system compensating for self-lucrative behaviours in water resource sharing.pdf
Title: A constrained multi-agent system compensating for self-lucrative behaviours in water resource sharing
Authors: Barbalios, N; Ioannidou, I; Tzionas, P; Paraskeuopoulos, S
Geographical_Context: Lake Koronia, Greece
Agricultural_Domain: Irrigation/water management; Shared water-resource management; Farmer behaviour
Study_Objective: Develop and validate a constrained multi-agent water-sharing model that represents self-interested farmers with no inter-agent communication/observation and tests a self-adaptive learning rule for preserving the shared resource and farmer viability.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Simulate farmer extraction of a shared irrigation-water resource under limited local knowledge and adapt individual water requests to reduce tragedy-of-the-commons behaviour.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; Algorithm; Coordination mechanism; Policy-evaluation framework
Agent_Types: Farmer/water-user agents
Agent_Roles: Each farmer independently selects a daily water-withdrawal action according to a behavioural policy and local feedback; the shared reservoir/environment returns water and state cues.
Decision_Mechanism: Self-adaptive learning rule; Non-rational policy; Profit-driven utility policy; Environment-friendly utility policy
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Farmers independently choose daily withdrawal quantities with no knowledge of other farmers and no direct communication; the proposed learning modifier adapts actions using own accumulated reward, local resource-state perception and experience.
Input_Information: Ideal water requirement; greediness factor; accumulated water/reward; perceived resource-state gradient; risk aversion and profit/environment weights; local experience
MAS_Platform_Technology: Custom computer simulation; implementation language NR
Coordination_Mechanism: Environment-mediated implicit coordination through the self-adaptive learning algorithm and shared-resource feedback; no direct inter-agent negotiation.
Communication_Mechanism: No direct inter-agent communication or observation; environment-mediated/indirect local feedback only.
Information_Shared: No agent-to-agent information; each farmer observes only its own accumulated water/reward and local cues about how quickly the resource is declining.
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Shared irrigation water / lake-reservoir resource
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Balance farmer water/profit needs with preservation of the shared water resource and long-term farmer/crop survival.
Conflict_Resolution: No explicit bargaining; resource conflict is mediated by reservoir depletion and the self-adaptive learning rule, which reduces excessive withdrawals and indirectly redistributes water availability.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Farmer agents drawing from the same finite water resource with heterogeneous greediness/self-interest.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Farmer ideal water need; previous water received; perceived reservoir-depletion gradient; greediness; behavioural policy; accumulated reward/experience
Agricultural_Outcomes: Farmer/crop survival rate improves when adaptive learning is used; the model represents whether irrigation received exceeds a crop-survival threshold.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Adaptive learning reduces wasteful over-extraction and distributes water more efficiently among farmers.
Environmental_Outcomes: Higher end-of-season shared-water level and improved preservation of the Lake Koronia-like resource under adaptive learning.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Self-adaptive reduction of excessive farmer withdrawals; environment-friendly behavioural policy; local feedback on reservoir depletion.
Quantitative_Results: Calibration against Lake Koronia data produced 1.56% average error. With adaptive learning, an average 3.7 times more water was preserved across policies and average farmer survival rate increased 2.15 times; the environment-friendly policy plus learning achieved the highest mean final water level (678 normalised units).
Tradeoffs_Reported: Farmer profit/survival vs water-resource preservation; without adaptive learning no tested policy simultaneously maximised farmer survival and preserved the shared resource.
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Model calibration/validation; Comparative policy evaluation
Evaluation_Environment: Shared self-contained irrigation-water resource calibrated to the Lake Koronia ecosystem and exploited by simulated farmer populations.
Data_Source: Real-world Lake Koronia water-level/agricultural observations for calibration; Monte Carlo-generated farmer populations/greediness assignments for simulation.
Experimental_Scenarios: Three farmer policies (non-rational, profit-driven, environment-friendly), each tested with and without the self-adaptive learning algorithm over systematically generated farmer populations.
Baselines_Comparators: Each policy without adaptive learning; comparisons among NR, PD and EF policies.
Evaluation_Metrics: Model calibration error; final water-resource level; farmer/crop survival rate.
Evaluation_Results: The model closely reproduced Lake Koronia depletion behaviour and adaptive learning improved both resource preservation and farmer survival across all three policies.
Evaluation_Scale: Multiple Monte Carlo-generated farmer populations across greediness categories; daily interaction over a cultivation season; exact fixed farmer count varies/is not reported as one single evaluation scale.
Limitation_Categories: Environmental modelling; Real-world validation; Other — simplified behavioural/resource assumptions
Reported_Limitations: Model assumes no inter-agent communication/observation, farmers cultivate the same crop type, and a self-contained resource with zero hydrological balance; results use normalised units. These assumptions simplify real stakeholder and hydrological heterogeneity.
Reported_Research_Gaps: NR
Extraction_Notes: Lack of communication is an intentional model constraint, not missing documentation. Coordination emerges indirectly through environmental feedback and the adaptive learning modifier.

PDF_Filename: Multi-agent task allocation for harvest management.pdf
Title: Multi-agent task allocation for harvest management
Authors: Harman, H; Sklar, EI
Geographical_Context: Commercial soft-fruit farm and small research farm; specific UK farm location NR
Agricultural_Domain: Harvest management; Agricultural workforce management; Soft-fruit production; In-field logistics
Study_Objective: Automate worker-to-field team formation, picker/runner composition and in-field picking/transport task allocation for soft-fruit harvesting using real farm data and multi-agent task-allocation methods.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Support harvest managers and team leaders by allocating workers to fields and assigning picker/runner tasks to reduce harvesting time, waiting and management effort while balancing workloads.
Contribution_Type: Algorithm; Coordination mechanism; Simulation model; Decision-support system
Agent_Types: Human-worker software agents; Picker agents; Runner agents; Auction manager/task-allocation component
Agent_Roles: Worker agents represent individual farm workers; pickers harvest fruit, runners transport full trays, and the auction manager allocates picking/transport tasks; higher-level algorithms form daily worker teams for fields.
Decision_Mechanism: Repaired/modified Round Robin team formation; workload smoothing; k-means worker modelling; Round Robin, Ordered Single Item and Sequential Single Item auctions
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Worker agents bid for and execute harvesting/transport tasks according to simulated capability and schedule, while central allocation algorithms/auction manager determine teams and task winners.
Input_Information: Estimated field yield; worker availability; historic/live picking speeds; fruit type/worker experience; field maps and task locations; picker capacity; navigation speed; task schedules
MAS_Platform_Technology: MASON discrete-event multi-agent simulation; market-based task-allocation algorithms
Coordination_Mechanism: Repaired Round Robin worker-to-field allocation; workload rebalancing; RR/OSI/SSI auction-based picker and runner task allocation
Communication_Mechanism: Auction manager advertises tasks, worker agents compute/send bids, and winning assignments are returned; central team-allocation component assigns workers to fields.
Information_Shared: Worker skills/picking speeds; estimated yield; task locations/fruit volume; agent schedules; bid costs; picker capacity and runner availability
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Seasonal human workforce; Worker-to-field assignments; Fruit-picking tasks; Tray/punnet transport tasks
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Reduce harvest execution/staff time and picker waiting while balancing workload, skill mix and worker-task suitability under limited seasonal labour.
Conflict_Resolution: Central scheduling/auction rules select winners by lowest task cost and rebalance field teams; tie-breaking and capacity/schedule rules resolve competing assignments.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Fields compete for a limited worker pool; picker and runner agents compete for harvesting/transport task assignments.
Agricultural_Outcomes: Harvest teams and in-field schedules are generated to complete soft-fruit picking more efficiently; direct crop-yield improvement is not measured.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Lower execution time, balanced workloads, reduced picker waiting, improved worker-task suitability and guidance on efficient picker/runner ratios.
Environmental_Outcomes: NR
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: NR
Quantitative_Results: RR3 produced the lowest worker-to-field execution time; for 2021, Actual vs RR3 staff time was about 2.97 vs 2.98 million seconds. In simulation, the best runner share was 57% for the 7-worker small field and 30% for the 102-worker large field; SSI for pickers with OSI for runners gave the shortest execution time.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Workload fairness vs execution/staff time; picker efficiency vs runner waiting; picker/runner staffing ratio vs total harvest duration.
Evaluation_Environment: MASON harvest simulation plus worker-to-field scheduling evaluated with commercial-farm historic/live data and a small research-field case.
Data_Source: Commercial soft-fruit farm: 2020 historical picking data and 2021 incrementally supplied live data; field maps, estimated yields, worker lists and recorded picking performance; small research-farm field data.
Experimental_Scenarios: Five worker-to-field allocation variants; multiple picker/runner ratios; RR/OSI/SSI picker and runner scheduling combinations; small and large field simulations.
Baselines_Comparators: Actual farm-manager teams; RR0/RR1/RR2/RR3 variants; RR, OSI and SSI task-allocation strategies.
Evaluation_Metrics: Execution time; staff time; percentage of workers assigned to unfamiliar fruit; max-min estimated picking time; picking-speed entropy; picker waiting time; max-min fruit picked.
Evaluation_Results: Proposed team allocations were comparable to or better than manually deployed teams; RR3 gave the best overall field-team execution time/balance, while SSI-picker/OSI-runner scheduling produced the shortest simulated in-field execution time.
Evaluation_Scale: Commercial farm: 175 picking days/25 fields in 2020 and 182 days/30 fields in 2021; large-field simulation used 102 workers; small research field used 7 workers.
Limitation_Categories: Real-world validation; Uncertainty; Computational requirements; Adoption/usability; Other — incomplete/prognostic farm data
Reported_Limitations: Live farm data can be incomplete and worker/yield forecasts uncertain; some simulation behaviours simplify real harvesting; schedules sent during 2021 testing were not operationally used; some scheduling modes are computationally expensive and worker preferences/environmental effects are omitted.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Compare additional task-allocation/evolutionary mechanisms; include worker preferences and weather/environment effects; run operational commercial-farm trials; improve yield prediction; evaluate hybrid human-robot harvesting workforces.
Extraction_Notes: Same harvest-workforce research family as S25/S34. This journal paper is the most extensive family member, combining team formation, picker/runner role selection and in-field task allocation with historic/live commercial-farm data.

PDF_Filename: Multi-Agent Task Allocation Techniques for Harvest Team Formation.pdf
Title: Multi-Agent Task Allocation Techniques for Harvest Team Formation
Authors: Harman, H; Sklar, EI
Venue: ADVANCES IN PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS OF AGENTS, MULTI-AGENT SYSTEMS, AND COMPLEX SYSTEMS SIMULATION. THE PAAMS COLLECTION, PAAMS 2022
Geographical_Context: Commercial soft-fruit farm; specific UK farm location NR
Agricultural_Domain: Harvest management; Agricultural workforce management; Soft-fruit production
Study_Objective: Compare genetic-algorithm and auction-based multi-agent methods for assigning seasonal workers to soft-fruit harvest teams using real commercial-farm data.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Form efficient harvest teams by assigning workers with heterogeneous picking skills to fields while balancing staff time and field completion time.
Contribution_Type: Algorithm; Optimisation method; Coordination mechanism; Decision-support method
Agent_Types: Human worker agents represented in the allocation model; Field bidder entities; Central allocation process
Agent_Roles: Workers provide heterogeneous picking capability and execute assigned fields; in OSI/SSI formulations fields bid for workers; the GA/auction process selects worker-to-field assignments.
Decision_Mechanism: Genetic Algorithm; Ordered Single Item auction; Sequential Single Item auction; multi-criteria fitness combining staff time and execution time
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Workers are modelled as assignable agents with individual picking speeds/experience, while a central optimisation/auction process determines team membership rather than workers independently negotiating assignments.
Input_Information: Estimated field yield; worker availability; recorded picking data; worker fruit-specific picking speeds/experience; labour-hour constraints
MAS_Platform_Technology: Jenetics genetic-algorithm library; auction-based task-allocation implementation
Coordination_Mechanism: Genetic optimisation of worker-field assignments; OSI/SSI auction-based allocation; comparison with repaired Round Robin
Communication_Mechanism: Auction-style field bids for workers within a central allocation process; explicit network/message protocol NR.
Information_Shared: Worker picking speed/experience; field estimated yield; worker availability; bid/fitness values; team assignments
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Seasonal human workforce; Worker-to-field harvest-team assignments
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Minimise average staff time and field execution time while ensuring every field receives workers and respecting limited worker availability.
Conflict_Resolution: GA fitness selection or auction winner rules resolve competing field demands for workers; tie-breaks favour fields with fewer agents and then higher yield.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Multiple harvest fields compete for a limited heterogeneous seasonal worker pool.
Agricultural_Outcomes: More efficient worker-to-field team plans are produced for soft-fruit harvesting; direct crop-yield improvement is not measured.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: GA produced the lowest estimated staff time and field execution time and offers substantial potential labour-cost savings.
Environmental_Outcomes: NR
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: NR
Quantitative_Results: GA achieved the lowest mean staff time and execution time among Actual, RR3, GA, OSI and SSI; execution-time differences were statistically significant. At £9.50/hour, the GA teams were estimated to save about £1,229.72 per day relative to the manual baseline based on mean staff time.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Staff time vs field execution time; solution quality vs GA computational run-time.
Evaluation_Type: Case study; Comparative evaluation; Computational experiment
Evaluation_Environment: Worker-to-field harvest-team allocation evaluated on real commercial soft-fruit farm data from the 2021 harvesting season.
Data_Source: Commercial farm 2021 data: 182 picking days, 30 strawberry/raspberry/cherry/blackberry fields, estimated yields, worker availability and recorded picking performance.
Experimental_Scenarios: GA tuning over selectors/population sizes/crossover/mutation settings; alpha weighting trade-off between staff and execution time; final comparison of GA, OSI, SSI, RR3 and actual farm-manager teams.
Baselines_Comparators: Actual farm-manager teams; repaired/modified Round Robin (RR3); OSI; SSI.
Evaluation_Metrics: Staff time; Execution time; GA fitness; statistical significance using Shapiro-Wilk and ANOVA.
Evaluation_Results: GA gave the lowest staff and execution times; staff-time differences were not statistically significant, but execution-time differences were significant. All tested methods produced schedules within a practically usable time window, although GA was slower.
Evaluation_Scale: 182 picking days; 30 commercial soft-fruit fields; entire 2021 seasonal workforce represented through daily worker lists.
Limitation_Categories: Computational requirements; Real-world validation; Other — seasonal/generalisation uncertainty
Reported_Limitations: GA takes longer to run than alternative approaches; seasonal variation in optimal GA settings is not yet examined; proposed teams were evaluated computationally rather than operationally deployed on the farm.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Study seasonal variation and adaptive GA population settings; gather farm-manager views on run-time; conduct real-world trials in which the commercial farm actually deploys the proposed teams.
Extraction_Notes: Same harvest-workforce research family as S25/S33. This paper focuses specifically on team formation and adds GA/auction comparisons using the same 2021 commercial-farm data line.
